explanation.text: A portfolio is a small, tidy collection of your best work with clear explanations. For you it can be your GitHub profile plus a few LinkedIn posts. You do not need a fancy website.

**How many projects?** Three good ones are enough. Choose projects that are different from each other, for example: a data cleaner, an AI helper, and a small tool you made for fun. Pin your best repositories on your GitHub profile so they show first.
**Each project needs a "front page".** Someone should understand it in one minute. That page is your README (see the LinkedIn module, lesson 4). It answers:

items: What is it, in one sentence?
How do I run it? (copy-and-paste steps)
What does the output look like? (a short example or screenshot with fake data)
What did you learn, and what would you improve next?

explanation.text: **Ready-to-share checklist.** Before you show a project to anyone:

items: It runs from a fresh folder using only the steps in the README.
It has a few tests, and they pass.
It handles bad input without a scary traceback.
There are no keys, passwords or real private data in the files or in the history.
The folder and the commit messages are tidy.

explanation.text: Be honest about what you did. If you followed a tutorial, say so, then say what you changed or added. Honest and specific is strong. Claims you cannot back up are not.
**Keep it alive.** Improve one project at a time and write a short post when you finish a step. Use the LinkedIn lessons: turn each project into a simple post with a link to the repository.

explanation.title: Portfolio entry
explanation.text: Use this for each project, in the README or in a LinkedIn Featured link. Fill in your own true details.
explanation.code:
[Project name]
[One sentence: takes X and gives Y for Z.]

Built with: Python, [libraries you really used]
Link: [repository address]

What it does:
- [feature 1]
- [feature 2]

What I learned: [one or two honest sentences]
What I would improve next: [one honest sentence]

examples.title: A weak entry and a better one
examples.code:
Weak: "Cool Python project. Check it out!"
Better: "Customer List Cleaner: a Python script that fixes names, phones and emails in a messy CSV file and writes a short report. Built with fake data. I learned to test edge cases like empty lines."

examples.title: A weak and a better "what I learned"
examples.code:
Weak: "I learned a lot about coding."
Better: "I learned to keep bad rows in a problems list instead of crashing, and to write a test before fixing a bug."

quiz.question: How many projects do you need for a start?
quiz.explanation: A few clear, different, finished projects show more than a long list of weak ones.

quiz.question: What is the first thing a project README should do?
options: Show a long history of your life
Say what the project is in one sentence
quiz.explanation: The first sentence tells the reader what it is, so they can decide quickly if they care.

quiz.question: You followed a tutorial to build a project. What is the honest thing to say?
options: Say you followed a tutorial and explain what you changed or added
quiz.explanation: Honest and specific is strong. Tutorials are a normal way to learn, and your own changes show your growth.
